name: Johannes Felsenberg
role: Group leader, Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel, Switzerland
background: His institutional biography records a Berlin PhD, Oxford postdoctoral work and an FMI group established in 2019. The group combines behavioral assays, targeted neural manipulation and imaging to examine memory re-evaluation.
works: Integration of Parallel Opposing Memories Underlies Memory Extinction
2018, Cell
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6198041/

Cue exposure without expected punishment recruits an opposing memory while an original aversive trace remains. Different MBON traces coexist; changed behavior is not evidence that the old trace was erased.
Re-exposure to reward re-evaluates related memories
2026, Current Biology; online 2025
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12881916/

Unpaired sugar re-exposure reduces related learned responses, with reward-specific and state controls. The measured reward trace in selected MBONs remains, distinguishing behavioral devaluation from disappearance of that trace.
fit: The prototype's persistent old choice could arise from trace competition or expression, rather than a simple inability to overwrite one number. These studies supply competing explanations to investigate, not a diagnosed cause of our failures.
question: What observation would distinguish a persisting old memory that competes with a new one from a failure to form the new association?
test: Proposed diagnostic: retain separate cue-evoked neural contrasts and behavior across acquisition, reversal and a later probe; include a control that never receives informative feedback. Any new neural mechanism would need identified circuits and a frozen prospective test.
limit: Extinction, reward devaluation and contingency reversal are distinct protocols. Neither cited result supplies a gamma4 reversal rule or a natural chess reward pathway.
connections: His 2018 study overlaps already-contacted Waddell and connectomics collaborators, as well as Périsse, who is newly added in this expansion. FMI currently lists Dennis Goldschmidt and Burak Guer as postdocs; membership alone does not establish individual project fit.
paragraph: Your work on memory re-evaluation made me reconsider what my failed reversals mean. In your extinction study, the old and new opposing memories coexist. Your recent reward re-exposure study also separates a changed learned response from disappearance of the measured memory trace. My model keeps choosing an old rewarded option in some runs. What would you measure first to distinguish an old memory competing with a new one from a failure to form the new association?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: when an old memory survives a changed choice
body:
Dear Dr Felsenberg,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. Chess and the public adult fly connectome led me to ask whether a model constrained by that wiring could learn useful decisions through experience and feedback.

Your work on memory re-evaluation made me reconsider what my failed reversals mean. In your extinction study, the old and new opposing memories coexist. Your recent reward re-exposure study also separates a changed learned response from disappearance of the measured memory trace. My model keeps choosing an old rewarded option in some runs. What would you measure first to distinguish an old memory competing with a new one from a failure to form the new association?

In six runs of a simple association experiment, the prototype preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three runs, so it failed the full test. This is an engineered prototype, and I haven't established whether its mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be open to occasional mentorship, starting with whether this question is a useful way to test the approach? I'd appreciate a candid assessment and can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

name: David Owald
role: Professor and research-group head, Institute of Neurophysiology, Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany
background: His current group links synaptic physiology, mushroom-body output and behavioral memory. This is useful for testing the location of persistent state rather than choosing a plasticity equation solely because it works.
focus: Postsynaptic memory mechanisms and behavioral readout
works: Postsynaptic plasticity of cholinergic synapses underlies the induction and expression of appetitive and familiarity memories in Drosophila
2022, eLife
https://elifesciences.org/articles/80445
Specific nicotinic receptor subunits and a postsynaptic scaffold contribute differently to induction and expression; the work provides evidence for postsynaptic plasticity at mushroom-body outputs.
Activity of Defined Mushroom Body Output Neurons Underlies Learned Olfactory Behavior in Drosophila
2015, Neuron
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.03.025

The paper links defined output pathways, altered odor responses and direct manipulations of approach/avoidance. It is indexed on the current author/lab publication page; direct full-text retrieval was unsuccessful.
fit: Our per-edge efficacy gain collapses several potential pre- and postsynaptic processes into one state variable. His work gives a concrete reason to ask what the model omits and how memory induction differs from expression.
question: Which experiment would expose a model that reproduces response changes but puts the lasting memory in the wrong physiological mechanism?
test: Proposed comparison: distinguish induction-only and retrieval-only perturbations in a future justified mechanism; measure both stored state and choice. Do not equate a software gain reset with a molecular receptor perturbation.
limit: The receptor experiments do not establish that gamma4 failures result from a missing receptor process. Reading coverage is deeper for the 2022 paper; verify the 2015 full text before using its detailed methods.
connections: Collaborations include already-contacted Waddell and Andrew Lin, who is newly added in this expansion. Carlotta Pribbenow is first author of the 2022 paper; her current role/contact has not been verified here.
paragraph: Your postsynaptic-plasticity study made me question where my model puts its memory. I currently save a gain on existing Kenyon-cell-to-output-neuron connections. Your results distinguish receptor subunits involved in forming a memory from those involved in expressing it, so a single saved gain may hide an important difference. What simple experiment would expose a model that produces a stronger response but puts the lasting change in the wrong physiological mechanism?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: where a reduced model stores its memory
body:
Dear Professor Owald,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a circuit model could learn to make better decisions from puzzles and feedback.

Your postsynaptic-plasticity study made me question where my model puts its memory. I currently save a gain on existing Kenyon-cell-to-output-neuron connections. Your results distinguish receptor subunits involved in forming a memory from those involved in expressing it, so a single saved gain may hide an important difference. What simple experiment would expose a model that produces a stronger response but puts the lasting change in the wrong physiological mechanism?

In six runs of a simple association experiment, the prototype preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the new option in only three runs, so it failed the full test. This is an engineered prototype, and I haven't established whether its mechanism is biologically sound. The chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be open to occasional mentorship, starting with whether this question is a useful way to test the approach? I'd appreciate a candid assessment and can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,

High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

name: Andrew Lin
role: Senior Lecturer, School of Biosciences, University of Sheffield, United Kingdom
background: The university profile records biology training at Harvard, a Cambridge PhD and an Oxford postdoc before Sheffield. His group studies how sensory representations support distinct memories, using physiology, behavior and computational models.
focus: Sparse coding, local inhibition and physiological variability
works: Localized inhibition in the Drosophila mushroom body
2020, eLife
https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/165904/7/elife-56954-v2.pdf
Local stimulation and volumetric imaging show spatially restricted APL activity and inhibition. Whole-cell labels do not imply a single uniform inhibitory signal.
Compensatory variability in network parameters enhances memory performance in the Drosophila mushroom body
2021, PNAS
https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/181348/1/Abdelrahman%20Lin%20Proceedings%20of%20the%20National%20Academy%20of%20Sciences%202021.pdf

A computational model tests compensation for heterogeneous excitability; predicted parameter relationships are compared with hemibrain anatomy. Performance benefits in this model are not evidence for our endogenous-learning mechanism.
fit: An adult connectome model can preserve edges yet distort cue selectivity through its activity and inhibition assumptions. This makes representation quality a plausible diagnostic before adding reward-omission machinery.
question: Which representation measurement would separate poor cue selectivity from an incorrect plasticity rule?
test: Proposed diagnostic: record per-cue KC activity distributions and overlap before learning, alongside lifetime sparseness across a prospectively selected cue set. Do not alter completed experiment gates or replace fixed wiring to force sparsity.
limit: The PNAS compensation models contain modeling choices, not a unique measured biological update rule. Spatial inhibition may require a more detailed physiological representation than our neuron-level state.
connections: Tom Cozens has already been contacted. These are colleagues within the same Sheffield group; another contact would share that lab context, not represent an independent referral.
paragraph: Your work on local APL inhibition and compensatory variability made me wonder whether my input representation is part of the problem. I preserve the graph, but that doesn't ensure that two cues activate distinct enough Kenyon-cell populations. Your modeling work checks how variability and compensation affect memory performance, which seems useful before I change the learning rule. Which representation measurement would you use first to separate poor cue selectivity from an incorrect plasticity mechanism?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: separating cue coding from learning
body:

name: Emmanuel Périsse
role: CNRS researcher (CRCN) and leader of Neural Circuits and Value Coding, Institute of Functional Genomics, Montpellier, France
background: His CNRS biography traces honeybee calcium/memory doctoral work, postdoctoral work in Worcester and Oxford, and founding a Montpellier team in 2018. The current lab focuses on how learned value guides later choices.
focus: Absolute versus relative value and interacting reinforcement systems
works: Differential coding of absolute and relative aversive value in the Drosophila brain
2022, Current Biology
https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(22)01380-X
Sequential aversive experiences recruit punishment and specific reward-associated pathways to encode relative value. A less bad outcome can be assigned a better-than value.
Integration of Parallel Opposing Memories Underlies Memory Extinction
2018, Cell; coauthor
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6198041/
Behavioral suppression of an old aversive response involves an opposing memory and integration in output circuits, rather than necessarily erasing the original trace.
fit: The project needs to distinguish an absolute teacher score from a comparison between possible outcomes. This is especially relevant before assigning one signed scalar to an arbitrary reinforcement population.
question: What small behavioral comparison would show that a model uses relative outcome value instead of merely preferring the option with a positive score?
test: Proposed task: compare two aversive outcomes and independently test each against a neutral cue, with balanced exposure and a matched uninformative-feedback control. Establish specific pathways before interpreting it as a fly value mechanism.
limit: Electric-shock and olfactory valuation experiments do not identify a pathway for chess scores. Our prototype cannot currently reproduce the full interacting appetitive/aversive network.
connections: Collaborates with previously-contacted Waddell; Miguel Pavão-Delgado is a 2022 co-first author and is currently listed as an FMI PhD student, so the old paper affiliation should not be reused as a contact.
paragraph: Your work comparing absolute and relative aversive value connects to a question I haven't resolved about feedback. A move can be worse than doing nothing but better than the available alternatives. Your study shows that comparing two aversive experiences involves interactions with reward-related pathways. I don't want to represent all those cases with one arbitrary signed signal. What small comparison would show that a model uses relative outcome value rather than just preferring a positive score?

name: Toshiharu Ichinose
role: Associate Professor, Frontier Research Institute for Interdisciplinary Sciences, Tohoku University, Sendai, Japan
background: The university timeline records an associate-professor appointment from April 2024. His research connects dopamine and recurrent memory circuits with cell-specific protein translation and consolidation.
focus: Recurrent reward feedback and memory stabilization
works: Reward signal in a recurrent circuit drives appetitive long-term memory formation
2015, eLife
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4643015/
Identified PAM-α1 and MBON-α1 circuitry contributes to appetitive long-term memory acquisition/consolidation; the circuit and receptor requirements provide more than a generic reward scalar.
Translational regulation enhances distinction of cell types in the nervous system
2024, eLife reviewed research
https://elifesciences.org/articles/90713

Cell-type RNA-seq/Ribo-seq analysis and reporter tests show translational differences between neurons and glia. It informs limits of deriving physiology directly from anatomical or transcript labels; it does not itself prove a memory-update mechanism.
fit: The current saved state persists because software retains it. His work supplies questions about recurrent reinforcement and stabilization that distinguish persistent storage from a justified biological memory process.
question: What minimal acquisition-versus-post-training comparison would test whether persistent memory needs a recurrent reward process?
test: Proposed prospective condition: selectively interrupt a justified recurrent pathway during training versus afterward, and test retention later. Mapping α1 in our released graph and specifying permitted state changes would precede implementation.
limit: The α1 result cannot be silently transferred to gamma4. Protein translation measurements should not be translated into invented molecular state variables without a justified reduction.
connections: Coauthored the 2015 study with previously-contacted Aso and Tanimoto. The current lab's broader molecular focus differs from their circuit-level outreach questions.
paragraph: Your study of a recurrent reward circuit made me think about what happens after a learning trial ends. My model stores a local synaptic gain, but its persistence comes from saving that value; I haven't shown a biological process that stabilizes it. Your current work on protein translation adds another reason not to infer physiology from wiring alone. What minimal comparison between training and the period afterward would test whether a simplified model needs recurrent reward processing to maintain a memory?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: what stabilizes a memory after training
body:
Dear Dr Ichinose,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a circuit model could learn to make better decisions from puzzles and feedback.

Your study of a recurrent reward circuit made me think about what happens after a learning trial ends. My model stores a local synaptic gain, but its persistence comes from saving that value; I haven't shown a biological process that stabilizes it. Your current work on protein translation adds another reason not to infer physiology from wiring alone. What minimal comparison between training and the period afterward would test whether a simplified model needs recurrent reward processing to maintain a memory?

name: André Fiala
role: Professor of Molecular Neurobiology of Behavior, University of Göttingen, Germany
background: The university profile records a Berlin PhD, research in New York and Würzburg, and the Göttingen professorship from 2008. The lab combines optical measurements and circuit manipulations to study learning and adaptive sensory processing.
works: Visualization of a Distributed Synaptic Memory Code in the Drosophila Brain
2020, Neuron
https://www.cell.com/neuron/fulltext/S0896-6273(20)30217-8
Imaging individually assigned KC boutons shows compartmental learning-related changes and decorrelation. Boutons, rather than a uniform cell-wide signal, can be modifiable units.
Optical Dissection of Experience-Dependent Pre- and Postsynaptic Plasticity in the Drosophila Brain
2015, Cell Reports
https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(15)00242-9
Targeted reporters distinguish presynaptic calcium, vesicle release and postsynaptic calcium. Prolonged odor experience changes these measures differently.
fit: Our simulation's neuron-level activity and per-edge gain should be evaluated against more than one output contrast. These methods show why response, release and postsynaptic changes are not interchangeable measurements.
question: Which independent synaptic observation would most clearly challenge a model that uses one scalar activity per neuron?
test: Proposed comparison: specify predictions for local bouton responses and cue separability in an untouched cue family. The full graph must remain sparse, and subcellular state would require a bounded-memory justification.
limit: Calcium signals are not identical to neurotransmitter release or the model's scalar activation. Do not claim that our fixed neuron-level model reproduces these spatial observations.
connections: His current project page addresses acuity learning and second-order conditioning; Bertram Gerber and Stephan Sigrist are research collaborators, not independently verified referral channels.
paragraph: Your imaging of individual Kenyon-cell boutons made me question a simplification in my model. I preserve neuron identities and connections, but use one activity value per neuron. Your studies distinguish local bouton changes and separate presynaptic calcium, release and postsynaptic responses. I want a test that could contradict my model rather than only confirm its own output. Which synaptic observation would most clearly expose a problem with that single-value representation?

name: Bertram Gerber
role: Head, Genetics of Learning and Memory, Leibniz Institute for Neurobiology; Professor of Behavioral Genetics, Otto von Guericke University, Magdeburg, Germany
background: His institutional biography describes honeybee learning doctoral work, establishing larval fly learning assays, Würzburg neurogenetics and the Magdeburg group. Current themes include reinforcement processing and memory-based expectations.
focus: Timing, punishment/relief and purposeful memory expression
works: Reinforcement signaling of punishment versus relief in fruit flies
2018, Learning & Memory
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5959229/

Defined dopamine-neuron stimulation supports different learned valences depending on cue timing. Punishment and relief effects are not equally dependent on dopamine biosynthesis, restricting a one-signal interpretation.
Functional architecture of reward learning in mushroom body extrinsic neurons of larval Drosophila
2018, Nature Communications
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-03130-1
Single-cell anatomy, connectomics and targeted manipulations distinguish neuron contributions to odor preference, taste preference and associative learning in stage-3 larvae.
fit: His work helps prevent our existing temporal response reversal from being confused with successful contingency reversal. It also treats the behavioral meaning of experimentally stimulated neurons as a question to test.
question: What behavioral control would distinguish a timing-induced valence change from adaptation to a newly reversed contingency?
test: Proposed design: orthogonally vary cue/stimulation order and which cue's action earns reinforcement, keeping informative-feedback and pulse-count controls separate. Freeze this new test before running it.
limit: The timing study's stimulation meaning is itself qualified; its identified cells and larval anatomy do not provide an adult gamma4 or chess mapping.
connections: Current institutional staff list includes Christian König-Bethke (postdoc), a collaborator on timing/relief work. Schleyer, Eschbach and Mancini from this collaboration network have already been contacted.
paragraph: Your punishment-versus-relief work connects to a distinction I need to keep clear. My prototype can change a response when cue and stimulation order are reversed, but that doesn't mean it can adapt when the rewarded option changes. Your experiments also show why the meaning of stimulation needs to be tested. What behavioral control would distinguish a timing-induced change in valence from learning a newly reversed contingency?

name: Andreas Stephan Thum
role: Professor of Genetics, Institute of Biology, University of Leipzig, Germany
background: His university profile records Leipzig appointment since 2017 and earlier work in Konstanz and Fribourg. The lab integrates behavioral neurogenetics, defined sensory reinforcement and larval connectomics.
works: Four individually identified paired dopamine neurons signal taste punishment in larval Drosophila
2025 final reviewed version; earlier 2023 version listed by lab
https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/91387/elife-91387-v1.pdf

Manipulations, imaging and connectomics distinguish contributions of four DL1 dopamine-neuron pairs to high-salt punishment. Optogenetic substitution and natural-stimulus necessity are different tests; the cited PDF is an earlier reviewed version.
Functional architecture of reward learning in mushroom body extrinsic neurons of larval Drosophila
2018, Nature Communications
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-03130-1
Maps nearly all 44 input/output/APL neurons in stage-3 larvae and tests their specific roles across sensory preference and associative-learning tasks.
fit: Before treating injected PAM activity as feedback, we need evidence that the targeted cells carry an appropriate teaching signal. His studies illustrate combining cell identity with separate functional necessity and sufficiency tests.
question: What minimum combination of natural-stimulus and stimulation controls would justify calling an identified population a teaching pathway?
test: Proposed evidence checklist: mapped identity, cue/stimulus responsiveness, reinforcement-substitution sufficiency and selective training-stage necessity. These are requirements for a future mechanism, not tests already passed by FlyChess.
limit: Larval DL1/pPAM cells are not interchangeable with adult FlyWire populations. Reviewed-preprint version/year differences must remain visible when citing the salt study.
connections: Gerber and already-contacted Schleyer, Zlatic and Cardona are coauthors of the 2018 study. No contact is inferred for its junior authors.
paragraph: Your work on individually identified larval dopamine neurons shows the kind of evidence I need before calling a population a teaching pathway. The salt-punishment study compares natural sensory input with targeted activation and inhibition, rather than relying only on an anatomical label. My graph is adult, so I know the larval mapping can't simply be copied. What minimum combination of those controls would justify a reinforcement target in a simplified adult model?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: evidence for an identified teaching pathway
body:

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a circuit model could learn to make better decisions from puzzles and feedback.

Your work on individually identified larval dopamine neurons shows the kind of evidence I need before calling a population a teaching pathway. The salt-punishment study compares natural sensory input with targeted activation and inhibition, rather than relying only on an anatomical label. My graph is adult, so I know the larval mapping can't simply be copied. What minimum combination of those controls would justify a reinforcement target in a simplified adult model?

name: Ilona Grunwald Kadow
role: Professor of Physiology and Director, Institute of Physiology II, University of Bonn, Germany
background: The current university biography records the Bonn appointment from January 2022. Her group studies how sensory experience, bodily needs and internal state influence decisions, using flies and mice.
focus: Motivation versus memory and state-dependent choice
works: A Neural Circuit Arbitrates between Persistence and Withdrawal in Hungry Drosophila
2019, Neuron
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6839618/
Hungry flies persist in unrewarded odor tracking; defined MBONs, dopamine and a feeding-related octopamine input influence persistence or withdrawal.
A dopamine-gated learning circuit underpins reproductive state-dependent odor preference in Drosophila females
2022, eLife
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9536836/
Mating-related sensory experience and dopamine/MBON manipulations influence lasting polyamine preference, with distinct contributions to induced changes and later expression.
fit: Choosing the old option can reflect state-dependent persistence as well as deficient association updating. Her studies offer a way to question the behavioral interpretation of our fixed decoder and reduced internal state.
question: What comparison would separate failure to update a learned association from persistence caused by motivational state?
test: Proposed diagnostic: compare learned choice and a separate engagement/persistence measure, while independently controlling internal state in a biologically justified model. Merely adding a parameter called hunger would not validate it.
limit: The prototype has no reconstructed natural motivational state. Food tracking and reproductive preference are different tasks from chess and from our engineered two-cue choice.
connections: Current official group roster includes Jean-François De Backer and Karen Cheng; both can be researched later, but this dossier does not assign them unverified independent projects.
paragraph: Your work on hungry flies persisting without reward made me think about another explanation for my model's old choices. A failure to switch could reflect persistence or internal state, rather than failure to learn the new association. Your reproductive-state study also separates lasting sensory experience from the later expression of preference. What comparison would you use to distinguish deficient memory updating from a motivational reason to keep choosing the old option?
subject: Student mentorship inquiry: persistence or a failure to update
body:
Dear Professor Grunwald Kadow,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I'm interested in neuroscience and decision-making, and chess gave me a question to explore: could a model using the adult fly connectome learn useful choices through experience?

Your work on hungry flies persisting without reward made me think about another explanation for my model's old choices. A failure to switch could reflect persistence or internal state, rather than failure to learn the new association. Your reproductive-state study also separates lasting sensory experience from the later expression of preference. What comparison would you use to distinguish deficient memory updating from a motivational reason to keep choosing the old option?

In six runs of a simple association experiment, the prototype preferred the rewarded option more after training.
